title: Israel Hostile Aircraft Alert in North Was False Identification, IDF Says
excerpt: Sirens over Zar'it and Shomera along the Lebanese border were a false identification, the IDF said, weeks after the flydubai FZ1073 incident prompted tighter airline crew screening.
body:
• An alert over a suspected hostile aircraft intrusion was sounded over Zar'it and Shomera in northern Israel, along the border with Lebanon.
  • The Israel Defense Forces said shortly afterwards that the warning was the result of a false identification, according to reporting by The Jerusalem Post, confirmed by a second Israeli news report the same morning.
  • No hostile aircraft was confirmed in the reports read; both accounts describe the incident as a false identification and The Jerusalem Post report calls it a developing story.
  • The alert comes weeks after flydubai flight FZ1073 on September 30 was diverted to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia after its co-pilot attacked the Indian captain, after which Israel introduced tighter crew-screening rules for airlines.

An alert over a suspected hostile aircraft intrusion along Israel’s border with Lebanon triggered alarm in northern Israel before the military clarified that it had been caused by a false identification, according to reports in The Times of India and The Jerusalem Post.

The alert was sounded over the areas of Zar’it and Shomera. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) issued a statement shortly afterwards confirming that the warning was the result of a false identification, The Jerusalem Post reported.

Second report confirms the same alert

The same sequence is confirmed independently of the Times of India account. The Jerusalem Post report republished by JBizNews states that an alert was sounded after a hostile aircraft intrusion was identified along the Lebanese border in northern Israel, over Zar’it and Shomera, and that the IDF released a statement shortly after the alarm stating that the alarm was a result of a false identification. The report describes the story as developing.

A separate Israeli live-news report the same morning carried the same finding in its own wording: Israel RealTime reported that hostile aircraft infiltration sirens sounded early that morning in the Zar’it and Shomera areas and that the alerts were subsequently determined to have resulted from a false identification.

None of the reports read names a specific aircraft or reports casualties or damage from this alert. Details beyond the alert and the IDF clarification should be treated as unconfirmed.

"Second report confirms the same alert The same sequence is confirmed independently of the Times of India account."

Why the flydubai incident frames this alert

The Times of India report places the alert weeks after an attempted hijacking of a flydubai flight carrying passengers from Dubai to Tel Aviv raised questions over aviation security and the screening of foreign airline crew members.

That earlier incident was aboard flydubai Flight FZ1073 on September 30. The flight, operating from Dubai to Tel Aviv, was diverted to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia after Omani co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami attacked Indian captain Smit Machchhar and attempted to seize control of the aircraft, the report says. Machchhar managed to unlock the cockpit door despite being injured, allowing passengers, crew members and two off-duty flydubai pilots travelling on the flight to intervene and overpower the co-pilot. The aircraft landed safely in Tabuk.

The United Arab Emirates later honoured Machchhar and the flight crew with the First Class Order of Zayed II for their actions during the incident, according to the same report. The award was conferred by UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and presented by Dubai Crown Prince Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum.

Tighter screening followed

In response to the security concerns after the flydubai incident, Israel introduced tighter screening requirements for airlines operating flights to and from the country, the report says. Under the new rules, carriers must submit crew details at least 48 hours before departure, with subsequent updates required no later than two hours before take-off and a final list at take-off.

The measures apply to incoming and outgoing flights operated by both Israeli and foreign airlines, and are intended to give authorities more time to conduct background checks, according to the report.

Separate weapons find in southern Lebanon

Separately, the IDF said on Thursday that its troops had uncovered more than 340 weapons belonging to Hezbollah during operations in the southern Lebanon Security Zone, the Times of India report says. Soldiers from the 188th Brigade of the 36th Division found the weapons in the Beaufort Ridge and Litani River areas. The recovered material included RPG rockets, anti-tank missiles, mortar shells, firearms, explosives and ammunition, according to the military.

The troops also discovered a tunnel shaft approximately seven metres deep inside a civilian home, containing medical and living equipment, the report says, citing the IDF.

No source read links that operation to the northern alert. The confirmed story is narrow: an alert sounded, and the military said it was a false identification.
